abstract: Background Primary hypertension in childhood tracks into adulthood and is associated with increased cardiovascular risk. Studies conducted in individuals aged <18 years, an age group without many of the confounding comorbid cardiovascular disease risk factors in adults, provide an opportunity to explore early cardiovascular target‐organ injury. Methods Youths (n=132, mean age, 15.8 years) were stratified by blood pressure (BP) as low–BP, mid‐BP, and high–BP and by left ventricular mass index as low‐and high left ventricular mass index. Systemic circulating RNA, microRNA, and methylation profiles in peripheral blood mononuclear cells and deep proteome profiles in serum were determined using high‐throughput sequencing techniques. In vitro cell culture experiments assessed angiotensin II‐ and microRNA‐mediated Vash1 (vasohibin‐1 protein) regulation and Vash1‐mediated hypertrophic response. Results In high‐BP youths, transcriptomics analysis identified 7 differentially expressed genes, including elevated VASH1 transcripts but correspondingly diminished levels of its microRNA (microRNA‐24‐3p and microRNA‐335‐5p). In vitro experiments revealed that either angiotensin II treatment, microRNA‐24‐3p or microRNA‐335‐5p overexpression, reduced endogenous VASH1 transcript levels. In contrast, exogenous Vash1 protein treatment induced cellular hypertrophy. Hypermethylation of GSE1 , POTE1 , and MN1 ; hypomethylation of MAD1L1 and SH3BP4 ; elevated Protein Z and diminished Superoxide dismutase 3 protein levels were observed in mid‐BP and high‐BP+high–left ventricular mass index groups. In youths with high–BP and high–left ventricular mass index, HYAL1 transcripts and Hyaluronidase 1 protein were elevated, suggesting the significant involvement of extracellular matrix in cardiovascular target‐organ injury. Conclusions The integration of multiomics data in this unique pediatric population during the early phase of high BP provides evidence of molecular changes that reveal both potential drug targets and strategies for ameliorating BP‐mediated cardiovascular target‐organ injury.

VASH1
microRNAs, Spearman correlation was used since RNA sequencing data are not normally distributed. Differentially methylated genes (DMGs) between 2 groups (mid‐BP [n=10] versus low‐BP+low‐LVMI [n=10] and high‐BP+high‐LVMI [n=10] versus low‐BP+low‐LVMI [n=10]) were determined using Fisher’s exact test. Based on the number of CpG islands and the depth of methylation in a pairwise comparison, we included only those differentially methylated regions (DMRs) that exhibited consistent methylation changes, either hyper‐ or hypomethylation, in at least 6 of the 10 pairwise comparisons to ensure robust and meaningful analysis. We excluded DMRs with equal hyper‐ and hypomethylation patterns across the comparison groups to avoid ambiguous results. Differentially expressed proteins (DEPs) between 2 groups (mid‐BP versus low‐BP+low‐LVMI and high‐BP+high‐LVMI versus low‐BP+low‐LVMI) were analyzed using Student’s
t

t

Clinical Perspective
What Is New?
Impairment of tissue angiogenesis that results from dysregulation of circulating antiangiogenic factors promotes target‐organ injury in youths with primary hypertension.
For the first time, we demonstrate the involvement of Vasohibin‐1 (intrinsic angiogenesis inhibitor) and Hyaluronidase1 (lysosomal enzyme) dysregulation in target‐organ injury among youths with primary hypertension in ventricular remodeling.
What Are the Clinical Implications?
Identification of key gene targets and specific pathways leading to early‐age hypertension‐mediated target‐organ injury will facilitate the development of therapeutic agents for clinical translation.
Attenuation of Vasohibin‐1 and Hyaluronidase1 expression to reduce pathologic ventricular remodeling could be a promising target for novel therapeutics to prevent and treat hypertensive cardiac injury.
Primary hypertension (PH) is a major risk factor for cardiovascular disease, affecting >1 billion people globally.
1
Chronic PH causes cardiovascular target‐organ injury (CV‐TOI), including left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH), renal disease, and neurologic injury, which can result in heart failure, end‐stage kidney disease, stroke, and cognitive dysfunction.
2
,
3
,
4
Understanding the pathophysiology of PH and PH‐associated CV‐TOI is essential if novel diagnostic and therapeutic strategies are to be developed. Despite worldwide prevalence, a high mortality rate, and substantial health care expenditures
2
related to PH, the actual mechanisms of PH and PH‐associated CV‐TOI are incompletely understood. Children and adolescents constitute an ideal population to study the origins of PH and its sequelae since elevated blood pressure (BP) is detectable in the young
5
,
6
and tracks into adulthood.
7
,
8
,
9
Its prevalence is increasing,
10
and up to 40% of youths have evidence of LVH when hypertension is first diagnosed.
11
Moreover, while CV‐TOI, such as LVH, is predictive of adverse hypertension‐related outcomes in adults, the molecular indications of early PH in youths, including the evolution of hypertension‐mediated cardiovascular injury in adolescence, remain unknown.
12
Preliminary studies in animal models and patients suggest that antiangiogenic factors are central to pathological cardiac remodeling in cardiomyopathies
13
,
14
,
15
,
16
and following ischemic injury.
17
Tissue angiogenesis has been shown to have antifibrotic and cardioprotective effects among individuals with abnormal cardiac remodeling.
18
,
19
,
20
Based on these studies, our objective was to explore whether circulating angiogenic factors could be dysregulated, both transcriptionally and epigenetically, in high BP and high left ventricular mass index (LVMI) as a measure of CV‐TOI in hypertensive youths.
By investigating a cohort of adolescent patients with and without elevated BP and LVH, the present study aimed to identify clinical and molecular predictors of CV‐TOI in circulation. This was achieved by integrating multiomics data and thus gain a better understanding of PH‐associated CV‐TOI in youth. Using transcriptomics data, we identified candidate genes and microRNAs involved in CV‐TOI. Furthermore, we investigated circulating DNA methylation profiles and protein profiles to determine the potential pathways and their contributions to the CV‐TOI process. Our results indicate that antiangiogenic
VASH1
and its predicted microRNAs were dysregulated at the transcript level. Additionally, in vitro experiments with H9C2 cells revealed that angiotensin II treatment results in reduced endogenous
VASH1
expression, while exogenous Vash1 (vasohibin‐1 protein) treatment caused cellular hypertrophy. Finally, using AC16, and HEK293T cells, we demonstrate that microRNA‐24‐3p and microRNA‐335‐5p posttranscriptionally regulate
VASH1
gene expression. Using methylation and protein profiles, we identified candidate genes involved in inflammation, oxidative stress, and extracellular matrix (ECM) degradation. Overall, based on the results from the present study, it can be concluded that increased BP is an early sign of molecular changes leading to the development of CV‐TOI.

VASH1
, which encodes a tubulin carboxypeptidase protein with antiangiogenic properties,
VASH2
encodes proangiogenic Vash2 protein, while
TTL
is translated to protein with tubulin tyrosine ligase activity. Significant positive enhancement of
VASH2
and
TTL
was only noted in the mid‐BP group; the expression of these genes decreased sequentially in the high‐BP group and then the high‐BP+high‐LVMI group, as expected. 2A
). Functional gene enrichment using Metascape revealed that pathways related to circulatory system processes, the vascular system, BP regulation, the transforming growth factor‐β signaling pathway, and muscle contraction were all enriched in upregulated (Figure

, Data Set
S3
) and downregulated gene sets (Figure
2C
, Data Set
S3
). Therefore, transcriptomic analysis identified

/

as a critical circulating factor with increased expression in response to BP, resulting in possible antiangiogenic signaling and tubulin carboxypeptidase activity. To evaluate whether the BP response regulates

expression in cardiomyocytes, H9C2 rat cardiomyocytes were treated with different concentrations of angiotensin II (0–10 μM) for 48 hours, mimicking hypertension‐induced cellular hypertrophy. As expected, angiotensin II caused cellular hypertrophy at 1‐ and 10‐μM concentrations (Figure
3A
and
3B
). However, the endogenous
VASH1
transcript and Vash1 protein levels displayed a trend of downregulation (Figure
3C
through
3E
), suggesting alternate, or secondary, mechanisms of Vash1 regulation in cardiomyocytes in response to angiotensin II. Further investigation revealed that Vash1 protein treatment induced cellular hypertrophy in H9C2 cells by significantly increasing their size (Figure
4A
and
4B
), whereas treatment of H9C2 cells with acute exogenous Vash1 protein for 24 hours at increasing concentrations (0–30 ng/mL) did not affect cellular viability (Figure

Discussion
In this observational study, we evaluated circulatory markers and associated signaling pathways putatively associated with CV‐TOI to explore the potential origins of sequelae related to high BP in youth. Specifically, to understand the regulation of circulatory factors in youth with high‐BP and high‐LVMI, a form of pathological cardiac remodeling, we analyzed PBMCs and serum samples from youths enrolled in the SHIP AHOY study. In our earlier report, we identified BP candidate genes and microRNAs using systemic in silico approaches
10
with the aim of determining if these genes were differentially regulated at epigenetic level in SHIP AHOY study participants. To accomplish this, we used molecular and pathway analysis via RNA sequencing, microRNA sequencing, global DNA methylation, and mass spectrometry. We selected subjects from low‐BP+low‐LVMI (n=10) and high‐BP+high‐LVMI (n=10) groups for initial RNA and microRNA sequencing analysis, and the DESeq2 package yielded unexpected results with no DEGs or differentially expressed microRNAs after adjusting for FDR. This was not improved by either increasing the sample numbers of low‐BP (n=42) and high‐BP (n=30) or additional analysis using Limma voom. Using a nominal
P
value threshold, we identified 7 common signature BP genes among which our analyses revealed a possible weak positive correlation between circulatory
VASH1
mRNAs and BP with resultant cardiac remodeling. The study participants comprise a pediatric population in early childhood hypertension with no specific symptoms of cardiac dysfunction to otherwise justify the observed RNA sequencing results and weak correlation with SBP and LVMI. Contrary to circulatory cells, cardiomyocytes exhibit diminished levels of endogenous
VASH1
transcripts upon angiotensin II treatment. This could be explained by the extracellular release of Vash1 to the circulation.
22
,
23
Vash1 lacks the classical secretion signal sequence and is considered an unconventional secreted protein. We next sought to determine the effect of Vash1 on cardiomyocytes. Cellular hypertrophy was observed when cardiomyocytes were incubated with Vash1 protein, explaining its deleterious effects on cardiac muscle cells.
Next, using microRNA sequencing data, we identified the downregulation of
VASH1
‐predicted microRNAs. In vitro overexpression of microRNA‐24‐3p and microRNA‐335‐5p diminished
VASH1
transcript and Vash1 protein levels. Further, these findings, along with methylation and proteomics data, highlight that
VASH1
is a likely key player in the pathological processes leading to the development of LVH in patients. Limitations of the Study
Our study has some limitations. For the given sample size of n=10 (high‐BP+high‐LVMI), our post hoc power analysis indicated that there was 80% power to detect a minimum FC of 5.6 at a significance level (FDR <0.01). Similarly, with n=35 (high‐BP), the minimum detectable FC was 2.5. Many gene expression studies use a threshold of 1.5 to 2 as a meaningful difference. The observed FCs in both groups were smaller than these thresholds, and they did not reach statistical significance after adjusting for false discovery. This suggests that while the study did not detect large expression differences, more subtle effects may have remained undetected due to inherent biological variability. Multiomics analysis of changes in molecular markers in youths with hypertension offers the advantage of identifying clues toward understanding the CV‐TOI process. However, whether the expression differences observed in these peripheral samples mediate effects within the target organ is unclear. In addition, the serum samples we obtained have broad heterogeneity, and the cellular composition of the blood was highly dynamic and confounding. Moreover, although our transcriptomic and proteomic data showed statistically significant results for DEGs and proteins, these values did not reach significance after adjusting for false discovery. This outcome is commonly observed in many transcriptomic analyses of human subject data with a minimal number of DEGs surpassing an FDR threshold, necessitating additional analysis using Limma voom.
62
,
63
Further application of various bioinformatics and statistics approaches are beyond the scope and objectives of the present study, and such data are publicly available and open to the research community for reanalysis. Another limitation of our study involves the highly dynamic cellular composition of the blood, which acts as a confounding variable when using PBMCs and circulatory proteins to assess circulatory epigenetic/protein biomarkers. Novel techniques, such as aptamer‐based proteomics, might be more advantageous than routine liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry for circulatory biomarker discovery. Thus, further studies are needed to validate our observations. While the present study in hypertensive youths sought to define basic aspects of disease progression at an early age, temporal dynamics, as CV‐TOI progresses, are essential to completely understand its evolution.
Conclusions
Our data suggest that PH in the presence of common intermediate phenotypes may lead to CV‐TOI in hypertensive youths through impaired angiogenesis mediated by circulatory
VASH1
, its microRNAs, and associated signaling pathways. Additionally, the deregulation of angiogenesis owing to upregulation of microRNA‐584‐3p, differential methylation of
VAV2
, elevated Platelet facor 4 variant and Superoxide dismutase 3 protein levels, as well as ECM degradation by Hyaluronidase‐1, might contribute to the pathological remodeling of cardiac tissues. The broad multiomics scope of this study provides initial evidence of global RNA and protein profiles in the circulation associated with hypertension in youths and identifies the likely involvement and deregulation of canonical pathways related to angiogenesis, inflammation, oxidative stress, and ECM organization. These findings suggest that such pathways may ultimately lead to cardiovascular dysfunction. Further research is warranted to use these multiomics findings to develop therapeutic interventions for CV‐TOI aimed at promoting angiogenesis and protecting against ECM degradation in patients with PH and to determine if these results are generalizable to other populations.
